title: ‘Far From the Trees’ Review: A Richly Contemplative Journey of Physical and Mental Meanderings, Beautifully Combining 4K Digital with Super 16
description: Language and sounds trigger idyllic childhood recollections in Meritxell Colell Aparicio’s deeply personal, contemplative drama “Far From the Trees,
body:
Language and sounds trigger idyllic childhood recollections in Meritxell Colell Aparicio’s deeply personal, contemplative drama “Far From the Trees,” a handsome reverie blending 4K, Super16mm and archival footage to capture the different textures of memory. Following a Mexican sound artist and her assistant-guide in the Peruvian Amazon as they record nature and indigenous languages, the film is a sensorial road trip of physical and mental meanderings that bisect life choices, parental ties and generational trauma. Aparicio resists drawing conclusions, privileging an experiential approach with its own rhythms, ambitious in scope yet intimate in focus, that could well become an arthouse sleeper.
	

	Already with her first film, “Facing the Wind” (which premiered in the Berlinale’s Forum), the director was exploring the conflicting emotions of adult children in relation to their aging parents, reflecting interior struggles closely connected to place. With “Far From the Trees,” premiering in competition at Locarno, she’s delved further into the psyche and its triggers, negotiating the mind’s tricky associations with both pleasurable and painful memories, and while Aparicio only skirts the way languages form distinct aural and visual concepts, her highly attuned feel for sounds greatly contributes to the film’s impact.


	Middle-aged Adela (Angélica Castelló, herself a sound artist and composer) is traveling through the forests of south-eastern Peru recording not only rapidly dying indigenous languages but even the trees themselves. Eager to engage with local populations and learn from her multilingual guide Lucho (José Luis López Cama), she has a certain gravitas that projects solitude, especially noticeable when first seen in the grey-blue light of early morning, staring out across a river at a restricted territory inhabited by uncontacted tribes. While we’re told that she’s a sound artist in Vienna, we never learn how she plans on using the recordings, possibly because that part of her inner journey lies in the future, whereas the film is focused on past and present.
	

	Flashbacks can be such tricky devices, especially when depicting an almost too-perfect earlier time, but Aparicio’s skills as editor (together with Ana Pfaff), and her choice of shooting the past in Super16mm, convey a subjectivity whose resonance suffuses Adela’s entire consciousness. Born in Mexico to a left-wing Catalan family, Adela’s spiritual and intellectual formation came from her grandparents, while her emotional nourishment was the realm of the housekeeper/nanny Paula (Teresita Sánchez). When the eight-year-old Adela is first seen cuddling with Paula, their bond is so tight that our assumption is she’s the mother; only gradually is it clear that grandmother Toni and grandfather Emili, both researchers working with sound, were more distant though loving figures, still deeply affected by the horrors of the Spanish Civil War.

	Adela stays in touch with Paula and Toni, now 98, via Zoom, but internet connections are unstable and she’s so wrapped up in her work and her reflections on the past that she’s not paying attention to her loved ones’ needs back in Mexico. Aparicio is not hard on Adela for this deafness, perhaps because there are so many links between the character and the director’s own history. As a single foreign woman living in Vienna, Adela has given up much to pursue her dreams, sustained by warmly lit memories of a quietly loving childhood, but she never seems to have questioned the power imbalance between her Spanish grandparents and their indigenous housekeeper, notwithstanding Paula’s status as an integral part of the family.

	It’s not clear whether Adela will ever have an epiphany about this dynamic, or the one that separates her from Lucho. Perhaps were Aparicio to show such a change, it would be too pat, too easy: Adela’s silences make her slightly inscrutable but also more real. As the child of an exiled family, she carries their burdens with her, the residue coloring her own status as a Mexican woman living in Austria and further cut off from her roots. Towards the end there’s a dreamlike montage of uncertain efficacy, though stunning images of Toni and young Adela on a bed covered in vines and grasses are so mesmerizing that the eye wants to linger further.

	Praise must go to production designer Anna Auquer, not just for that memorable sequence but the perfection with which she has created Adela’s crowded family home, where each object radiates meaning known only to its residents. Cinematographer Julián Elizalde brings an artist’s eye to lighting and feels equally at home with the diverse tonalities registered in both digital and Super16mm. An added layer is given via archival footage of anti-Franco exiles leaving Spain, silent witnesses to a rupture whose echoes are still being felt.

schema.headline: ‘Far From the Trees’ Review: A Richly Contemplative Journey of Physical and Mental Meanderings, Beautifully Combining 4K Digital with Super 16

title: David Letterman to Interview Matt Damon, Julia Roberts and More in ‘My Next Guest’ Season 7
description:
David Letterman‘s next guests who need no introduction are Matt Damon, Julia Roberts, Jimmy Kimmel and Alex Honnold.

	The late-night legend will si
body:
David Letterman‘s next guests who need no introduction are Matt Damon, Julia Roberts, Jimmy Kimmel and Alex Honnold.

	The late-night legend will sit down with the aforementioned subjects for longform interviews as part of his Netflix talk series, “My Next Guest Needs No Introduction With David Letterman,” which returns for Season 7 later this year.

	The sixth season of the show is currently up for an Emmy for outstanding hosted nonfiction series or special.
	

	Damon is deep into his press tour for the soon-to-be awards heavy “The Odyssey,” while Roberts is not currently promoting a project. Kimmel is on summer break between seasons of “Jimmy Kimmel Live!,” and surely the two outspoken late-night hosts will discuss CBS’ cancellation of “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert.” “Free Solo” subject Honnold recently completed his death-defying “Skyscraper Live” climb on Netflix. 


	“My Next Guest” has aired 31 episodes across six seasons and four specials, hosting esteemed interview subjects including Barack Obama, Tina Fey, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Jay-Z, Robert Downey Jr., Volodymyr Zelenskyy, John Mulaney, Michael B. Jordan, Miley Cyrus, Caitlin Clark, Billie Eilish and Adam Sandler. The series has received eight Emmy nominations across its six seasons, winning one in 2024.

	Executive producers of the series are Tom Keaney and Mary Barclay for Worldwide Pants; and Justin Wilkes, Michael Steed, Isabel Richardson and Yolanda T. Cochran for Jax Media/Imagine Entertainment. The producers are Tommy Alter, John Nemeth and Hunter Speese for Jax Media/Imagine Entertainment. The show is produced by Jax Media/Imagine Entertainment and Worldwide Pants, Inc.

schema.headline: David Letterman to Interview Matt Damon, Julia Roberts and More in ‘My Next Guest’ Season 7

title: ‘How Long Gone’ to Host Inaugural Awards Show ‘The Goneies’ in New York (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Move over, Oscars: There’s a brand new awards show for bicoastal elitists.

	“How Long Gone,” the cult-famous culture podcast hosted by Chris Black
body:
Move over, Oscars: There’s a brand new awards show for bicoastal elitists.

	“How Long Gone,” the cult-famous culture podcast hosted by Chris Black and Jason Stewart, has announced the inaugural edition of “The Goneies,” an intimate awards show taking place on Sept. 15 at Racket NYC in Manhattan. A limited number of tickets will go on sale at 9 a.m. ET here.

	Grammy-winning producer Brad Cook (Waxahatchee, Bon Iver) will serve as bandleader and musical director of the show, which will feature celebrity guests and surprise music performances. While specific details about “The Goneies” are limited, one might envision the “Las Culturistas Culture Awards” but straight — or, rather, for people whose Mariah Carey is Hamilton Leithauser. 
	

	Presented by Talkhouse, “The Goneies” marks the latest extension of the “How Long Gone” brand, which includes the podcast with more than 1,000 episodes, live performances, parties and red carpets hosted by Black and Stewart. In February, the duo announced “How Long Gone Today,” a video format of the show shot at a news-desk studio in Los Angeles.

	“This will be a seismic gathering of the greatest minds of our generation,” said Black and Stewart in a statement. “People who make music, post selfies, act, think they are funny, the media elite, and most of all look hot will all gather in one room in Manhattan to receive awards based on merit and high achievement from a podcast that they may or may not even listen to. We will have several surprise guests standing in with our all-star house band led by Brad Cook, so if nothing else, you get to see one of your faves play a few songs.”
	

	“To our knowledge, this is the first and only cultural awards show presented by a podcast, and we’re very proud of that,” added Talkhouse founder Ian Wheeler (a “Culturistas” dig!). “We’re also really excited to get Chris and Jason and all of their friends in front of a step-and-repeat for the very first time.”

schema.headline: ‘How Long Gone’ to Host Inaugural Awards Show ‘The Goneies’ in New York (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Stranger Things’ Star Noah Schnapp to Make Stage Debut in London (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
From the Upside Down of Hawkins to the boards of London. 

	Noah Schnapp, best known as Will Byers in “Stranger Things,” is set to make his world st
body:
From the Upside Down of Hawkins to the boards of London. 

	Noah Schnapp, best known as Will Byers in “Stranger Things,” is set to make his world stage debut in the British capital. 

	The actor, who became a household name thanks to the Netflix phenomenon, is adding theater to his resume as the star of “Affluenza” at Riverside Studios as part of its Mainstage Season 26/27. 


	Written and directed by Mainstage Season artistic director Andy Sandberg and running Sep. 26 to Nov. 21,  “Affluenza” is set against the ultra-wealthy social haven of the Hamptons, and is described as raising “thought-provoking questions about moral accountability, family legacy, and the American justice system.”
	

	In the play, when a teen’s drunken car ride ends in devastation, the verdict comes down to one question – is it possible to be too affluent to know the difference between right and wrong? Inspired by true events surrounding a shocking legal defence, “Affluenza” explores the “ripple effects of power and privilege.”

	“I am so excited to make my stage debut in London with ‘Affluenza,'” said Schnapp. “I started talking with Andy Sandberg a few months ago about finding the right opportunity to work together, and it’s thrilling to now be bringing this play to life in London. I wanted to be very intentional about what I took on next, and as I spend more time with this excellent script, I feel so connected to the characters. Without giving away too much, I get to play two very different roles, and it’s a story that’s really going to leave audiences talking and thinking.”
	

	“Affluenza” opens Riverside’s Mainstage Season 26/27, which comprises five new plays, largely set in contemporary America and exploring globally relevant themes.

	“I am incredibly excited to be launching this play and this season in just a few weeks — and now with Noah Schnapp at the helm,” said Sandberg, a Tony-winning producer who also serves as Mainstage Season artistic director. “Noah is a brilliant young actor who has captivated audiences on screen, and now London audiences will have the opportunity to see him in his stage debut. I’m honoured that Noah has connected with the script, and I think it speaks volumes that he has chosen an original play for his stage debut.”

	Following “Affluenza” the season will continue with “Sacrilegious,” by Tom Schulman, the Oscar-winning writer of “Dead Poets Society” and “Honey, I Shrunk the Kids,” and “Expecting,” by Scott Elmegreen and Drew Fornarola. Both are being are directed by Sandberg, who also serves as artistic director for the Hermitage in the U.S. Further productions and casting will be announced soon.

	Tickets for “Affluenza” are now on sale.

schema.headline: ‘Stranger Things’ Star Noah Schnapp to Make Stage Debut in London (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Actor Dylan Walsh ‘in Trouble’ After Saying on Cameo That 12 New Episodes Are Being Shot: I’m ‘Stepping Away’ From the Platform
description: “Heated Rivalry” actor Dylan Walsh has found himself on thin ice after revealing details about upcoming episodes in a video clip that has gone viral
body:
“Heated Rivalry” actor Dylan Walsh has found himself on thin ice after revealing details about upcoming episodes in a video clip that has gone viral.

	Walsh, who plays David Hollander on the hit hockey romance, recently paused his account on the celebrity video app Cameo after he got “in trouble” – in his words – for over-sharing in a clip about the upcoming second season of the series, which just began filming.


	“Getting ready to go back up to Canada and shoot some more episodes… so, I think we’re doing 12 this time,” Walsh says in a clip, posted on X, taken from a video recorded for a fan on Cameo.
	

	As creator Jacob Tierney has said that he doesn’t want to make more than six episodes per season, Walsh’s comment possibly implies that the production is filming Season 2 and Season 3 together, or that Season 2 would be split in half, according to some fans.

	“I don’t need to do 10 [episodes in a season],” Tierney told the Los Angeles Times in February. “I would always rather tighten the belt than get loosey-goosey. I would rather be like, ‘Let’s see how much story we can pack into these episodes.’”

	According to Entertainment Week, a note on Walsh’s Cameo account stated that it’s unavailable for personalized videos until August 2027, and the actor posted a message under his profile on the app that said, “Stepping away because a video went viral that got me in trouble.” Both notes have since been removed. 

	As EW notes, Walsh’s slipup could prove ironic as Rachel Reid’s novel “The Long Game,” from which the second season is adapted, includes a plot point around a video going viral on a Cameo-like app.
	

	The show follows two rival professional ice hockey players, Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie), who are in a secret relationship. Walsh plays Shane’s dad, who learns of their love affair when he walks in on them kissing in the Season 1 finale.

	Season 2 is expected to premiere in the spring of 2027.

	Variety has reached out to a rep for Walsh, who also appeared in “Nip/Tuck.”

schema.headline: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Actor Dylan Walsh ‘in Trouble’ After Saying on Cameo That 12 New Episodes Are Being Shot: I’m ‘Stepping Away’ From the Platform

title: ‘Othello’ Royal Shakespeare Company Adaptation Starring Sharon D. Clarke Postponed as She Undergoes Cancer Treatment
description: The Royal Shakespeare Company has postponed its production of “Othello,” with Sharon D. Clarke set to play the title role, so the actor can undergo
body:
The Royal Shakespeare Company has postponed its production of “Othello,” with Sharon D. Clarke set to play the title role, so the actor can undergo treatment for cancer. 

	The show had been scheduled to run Feb. 13 through April 3, 2027, at the Swan Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon.

	Touko’s staging reimagines the Shakespeare tragedy with a focus on misogynoir.


	Touko said the creative team sends Clarke love for her ongoing treatment and recovery. She called Clarke “the ultimate collaborator,” saying her generosity and passion for the project continues to astound her, and that she looks forward to reuniting with Clarke to bring the production to audiences when the time is right.
	

	RSC co-artistic directors Daniel Evans and Tamara Harvey said Clarke’s casting is integral to Touko’s adaptation, which is why the company made the difficult decision to postpone the run and give Clarke the space she needs for treatment. Describing Clarke as “a warrior,” they said they expect her to meet the challenge with the same strength and spirit she brings to her life and work, and that the RSC looks forward to revisiting the production in future, sending Clarke love and strength for a full recovery.

	Clarke thanked the RSC for its support. “Othello will be my north star as I undergo treatment,” she said, adding that she and her family have been humbled by the outpouring of support they have received.

	The RSC said ticket holders impacted by the postponement will be issued automatic refunds, with news on replacement programming for the slot to follow.

schema.headline: ‘Othello’ Royal Shakespeare Company Adaptation Starring Sharon D. Clarke Postponed as She Undergoes Cancer Treatment

title: The Cure Plays the Hits — and Robert Smith Tears Up at ‘Just Like Heaven’ — in Nostalgic, Whimsical Øyafestivalen Set: Concert Review
description: For the first five minutes of the Cure‘s headlining set at Øyafestivalen in Oslo, Norway, Robert Smith stared out at the packed crowd and smiled.
body:
For the first five minutes of the Cure‘s headlining set at Øyafestivalen in Oslo, Norway, Robert Smith stared out at the packed crowd and smiled. 

	As the band played the long, atmospheric introduction to “Alone” — the opening track of their great 2024 album “Songs of a Lost World” — Smith stood there positively beaming, hands clasped awkwardly in front of his usual all-black outfit. It’s a marked change in disposition from the last time I saw the Cure perform at the Hollywood Bowl in 2023, as part of their first North American tour in seven years. That set, though transcendent, had an air of nervousness to it as the band debuted the songs that would become their 14th album. Smith also seemed to be grappling with his own mortality, delivering several monologues throughout the night about growing older and time slipping by. Now, the frontman seems to have embraced it — and having previously said the Cure would retire in 2029 timed to the band’s 50th anniversary, he’s making the most of the time they have left. 
	

	On Wednesday night in Oslo, that meant delivering a hit-filled, two-and-a-half hour set in which Smith’s own whimsical spirit was on full display. After “Alone,” the show got off to a strong start with the 1989 classic “Pictures of You”  — the perfect example of the Cure’s happy music/sad lyrics modus operandi — followed by a zany rendition of “High” (during which Smith delightfully mimed the “bite my fingers through” line) and the soul-touching “Lovesong,” which got the crowd singing along. 


	It’s the same four-strong stretch the Cure has been employing for most of their prolific festival run this summer, but afterwards the band found ways to switch it up, adding the pleasant surprise of “Alt.End” and “The Last Day of Summer” from the early aughts. How Smith’s voice still sounds the same it did in 1979 — velvety smooth and without a single crack, unless he wills it to happen — should really be studied. And the band — including bassist Simon Gallup, keyboardist Roger O’Donnell, drummer Jason Cooper and guitarist Reeves Gabrels — is as tight as ever, as if they could play these songs in their sleep (at this point, they probably could). 
	

	Though Smith seemed in high spirits, the set hit an emotional peak after “In Between Days” and “Just Like Heaven” were played back to back. As the final notes of “Just Like Heaven” rang out, Smith took a moment to wipe tears from his eyes. “It’s strange, that song,” he said to the crowd, his voice wobbling. “Every now and then, that last bit…” Smith trailed off, but again smiled. Perhaps they were happy tears. 

	Cutting through the emotion, “Seventeen Seconds” tracks “Play for Today” and “A Forest” provided a spotlight for the band to jam out, with Smith and Gallup standing back-to-back for a slowed-down intro to the latter that built to a satisfying groove. That momentum stayed through “Wish” epic “From the Edge of the Deep Green Sea,” with Smith waving his hands around to accompany his devastating lyrics, ever the master storyteller. The set closed with “Endsong,” the final track of “Songs of a Lost World,” and the only other song from their new album the band would play. Hearing it mixed in with so many hits from over the years, it became clear just how cohesive the new record is with the rest of their discography — not an easy feat for a band that’s been around for nearly half a century. 

	Though they then briefly went off stage, the set was far from over. The Cure proceeded to deliver a stacked 10-track encore, during which Smith really let loose. In “Lullaby,” he performed as if the spider from the song was actually climbing up his body, ending the tune by pretending to eat it. During “The Lovecats,” he pawed around and hissed, and “Close to Me” prompted him to leave his guitar behind and walk from one side of the stage to the other, hopping and dancing around like a goth fairy.

	Introducing the final track, Smith injected some humor: “This is a new song, it’s called ‘Boys Don’t Cry.'” His earlier display of emotion made the song’s meaning hit even harder — and as the crowd erupted into jumps and shouts of glee, Smith stood there, a grin growing on his lipsticked mouth.

	See the full setlist below.

	“Alone”

	“Pictures of You”

	“High”

	“Lovesong”

	“Burn”

	“Fascination Street”

	“Never Enough”

	“Alt.end”

	“Push”

	“In Between Days”

	“Just Like Heaven”

	“The Last Day of Summer”

	“A Night Like This”
	

	“Secrets”

	“Play for Today”

	“A Forest”

	“From the Edge of the Deep Green Sea”

	“Endsong”

	ENCORE

	“Lullaby”

	“Wrong Number”

	“The Walk”

	“Mint Car”

	“The Lovecats”

	“Let’s Go to Bed”

	“Friday I’m in Love”

	“Close to Me”

	“Why Can’t I Be You?”

	“Boys Don’t Cry”

title: ‘Drishyam’ Producer Panorama Studios Invests in Indian Vertical Streaming Platform Rocket Reels (EXCLUSIVE)
description: India’s Panorama Studios, the producer behind the Bollywood “Drishyam” franchise, has invested in Indian original stories vertical platform Rocket R
body:
India’s Panorama Studios, the producer behind the Bollywood “Drishyam” franchise, has invested in Indian original stories vertical platform Rocket Reels, fueling the platform’s next phase of growth and global expansion.

	Panorama Studios is chaired by veteran film producer Kumar Mangat Pathak and led by filmmaker and managing director Abhishek Pathak. The studio has built a slate that includes “Omkara,” “Special 26,” “Pyaar Ka Punchnama,” “Raid,” “Shaitaan” and the “Drishyam” franchise, earning more than 50 awards. Abhishek Pathak directed “Drishyam 2” and is directing and producing “Drishyam 3,” due in theaters Oct. 2.
	

	Panorama Studios’ backing is expected to deepen Rocket Reels’ slate of programming, bolster its tech infrastructure and speed up output of new original series. The deal comes as vertical storytelling gains traction as one of digital entertainment’s fastest-growing formats.


	Founded by Kranti Shanbhag, Rocket Reels was among the first movers in India’s vertical streaming category, building a catalog that ranges across thrillers, romance, crime, mystery, sci-fi, horror and comedy. The platform is built for viewers on mobile devices, packaging its stories into brief, emotionally charged episodes.

	The platform offers stories in six Indian languages: Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Bengali and Gujarati. It has also expanded beyond India and is now available in 10 countries, including the U.S., the U.K., Canada, Australia, the U.A.E., Singapore, Malaysia, Bangladesh, Nepal and South Africa.

	Kumar Mangat Pathak, chair of Panorama Studios, said, “At Panorama Studios, we have always believed that compelling stories will find an audience, regardless of the format. Rocket Reels has built a strong platform that understands the evolving viewing habits of today’s digital-first consumers while staying rooted in quality storytelling.”
	

	Abhishek Pathak, managing director of Panorama Studios, said viewing habits are shifting quickly and that vertical storytelling is becoming a major format for viewers who consume content primarily on their phones. “Rocket Reels has built an innovative platform backed by compelling storytelling and a clear vision for the future. We are excited to partner with them as they redefine short-form entertainment and expand their reach across India and global markets,” he said.

	Kranti Shanbhag, founder of Rocket Reels, said the company set out from the start to tell engaging stories in a format built around how people actually live and consume media today. “Panorama Studios’ investment is a strong validation of that vision,” he said. “Their belief in our journey gives us the confidence and resources to create even more original, high-quality stories while expanding our reach across India and international markets.”

schema.headline: ‘Drishyam’ Producer Panorama Studios Invests in Indian Vertical Streaming Platform Rocket Reels (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Warrior Cats’ Animated Series Debuts First Footage, Character Model at Tencent Video Event
description: Tencent Video pulled back the curtain on its “Warrior Cats” animated series, showing fans early animation and character artwork for the first time a
body:
Tencent Video pulled back the curtain on its “Warrior Cats” animated series, showing fans early animation and character artwork for the first time at a fan meeting held in Shenzhen.

	Series director Rodrigo Blaas appeared alongside Zhou Wang, head of Randong Studio Group and vice president of content production at Tencent Video, offering fans a behind-the-scenes look at how the adaptation has come together creatively.


	That source material, books written under the pen name Erin Hunter, follows four Clans of wild cats bound by a code handed down from their warrior ancestors, as one Clan comes under threat from a rival and its warriors begin dying under suspicious circumstances. At the center of the story is Rusty, an ordinary housecat who joins the Clan and eventually rises to lead it.
	

	A centerpiece of the event was a 3D character model of Rusty, personally built by Blaas and unveiled to the crowd for the first time. It gave attendees a hands-on sense of how the cats from the book series are being reimagined for the screen.

	Tencent Video also debuted an exclusive work-in-progress screening at the event, giving fans their first public glimpse of the animated characters and environments and an early sense of the show’s visual direction.

	For Blaas, the physical model offered a way to work through the characters outside the screen as the animation develops. At the same event, Blaas walked fans through his approach to adapting the “Warrior Cats” universe into animated form and discussed how the series has taken shape creatively.

	Original Force is animating the series on behalf of Tencent Video. A.C. Bradley is showrunner, with Blaas directing. The creative team is drawing directly on the books’ characters and plotlines, using the first book arc, “Warrior Cats: The Prophecies Begin,” as its foundation.
	

	The series is set to launch in 2028 across Tencent Video’s platforms in China and Southeast Asia.

	Tencent Video counts itself among China’s leading streaming platforms, carrying a broad slate of content that spans drama series, animation, film, variety programming, sports and documentaries, alongside an expanding international footprint. The company has leaned into original productions in recent years, distributing its shows across multiple devices domestically while pushing Asian content out to audiences abroad through its overseas streaming arm.

schema.headline: ‘Warrior Cats’ Animated Series Debuts First Footage, Character Model at Tencent Video Event

title: San Sebastián Co-Production Forum: Celina Murga, Mariana Rondón, Matias Mariani, Santiago Loza and Christopher Murray Among Selected
description: Some of Latin America’s greatest arthouse directors –Celina Murga, Mariana Rondón, Santiago Loza, Matias Mariani and Christopher Murray– feature amo
body:
Some of Latin America’s greatest arthouse directors –Celina Murga, Mariana Rondón, Santiago Loza, Matias Mariani and Christopher Murray– feature among 15 projects set to be unveiled at San Sebastián’s 2026 Europe-Latin America Co-Production Forum, the Spanish festival’s biggest industry centerpiece.

	The selection also frames hot emerging director such as Ernesto Martínez (The Devil Smokes”) and first features which are sure to create interest. One case in point: Selma Cervantes’ “Mourning Sound,” set up at Teorema, founded by Michel Franco and partner Eréndira Núñez Larios and behind award-winning films such as “Memory,” “New Order,” “Heroic,” “Flies,” “Chronic” and “From Afar.”
	

	Galvanised by new and emerging talent, the 2026 lineup also serves as a tribute to what outgoing San Sebastián Festival director José Luis Rebordinos has achieved with the Forum: Consolidating it as Europe’s most significant Latin American meet and mart when a presence at co-production platforms has become ever more essential for the survival of so many Latin American filmmakers.


	Selected for the Forum, “The Rehearsals” marks Murga’s follow-up to “The Freshly Cut Grass,” presented by Martin Scorsese and a Tribeca best screenplay winner, and Murga’s fourth fiction film – after “Ana and the Others” (2003), “A Week Alone” (2007) and Berlin competition contender “The Third Side of the River” – films often displaying a large sense of place and unspoken but keenly observed emotions.

	Mariani impressed highly with his Berlin Panorama title “Shine Your Eyes,” a Netflix pick-up for the world. “‘Nature Boy’ began when I asked myself: what would it be like to be the father of an alien?” Mariani told Variety of his new Forum project.
	

	Rondón, behind another 2026 Forum project, “Looking for Sam,” won San Sebastián’s top Golden Shell in 2013 with “Bad Hair,” and, more recently, “It Would Be Night in Caracas,” a gripping thriller, Variety said, with Edgar Ramírez (“American Crime Story”) and Natalia Reyes (“Terminator: Dark Fate”).

	San Sebastián-bound with “Giant Stones,” Murray competed in Venice 2016 main competition with “The Blind Christ” and at Sundance with “Sorcery” in 2024.

	“The Amateurs,” (“Los Inexpertos,” Felipe Solari Yrigoyen, Chile, Argentina)

	Produced by Chile’s Quijote Films (“The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo”) and Argentina’s Gentil Cine, and set at an eccentric convention populated by people dressed as iconic movie characters where the original Maltese Falcon statuette vanishes along with a mysterious Russian guest. “The Amateurs” shows “how ordinary people, in a remote corner of South America and far from Hollywood, are forced to step up when circumstances spiral beyond their control,” says Solari about his potential feature debut.



	

									‘Ash Mother’
	



	“Ash Mother,” (“Mamá Ceniza,” Tana Gilbert, Chile-Germany)

	Blending archival research with hand-drawn rotoscoping, Gilbert’s follow-up to “Malqueridas,” Grand Prize winner at Venice Critics’ Week 2023, revisits a mother who killed her daughters during Chile’s nitrate crisis. Producer Paola Castillo says the technique creates “an ethical distance, without revictimizing.” Chile’s Errante produces with Germany’s Dirk Manthey Film, in a project connecting that historical case with mothers facing similar judgments a century later.

	“Diario Inconsciente,” (Santiago Loza, Argentina-Uruguay)

	Thirty years after a young man entered psychiatric hospitalization carrying a notebook and camera, Loza reconstructs those days through documents and recreations, rooted in a deeply personal experience from his own youth. Varsovia Films produces with Uruguay’s Monarca Films, while Compañía de Cine has boarded international sales. Now finalizing its script and financing, the project is, in Loza’s words, “a poetic tale of survival” that also explores mental health, friendship and filmmaking.

	“Dirty Face,” (“Cara Sucia,” Ignacio Acconcia, Spain-Uruguay)
	

	Ayhe Productions and Kabiria Films back Acconcia’s fiction feature debut, following Bruno, a Black teenager with vitiligo sentenced to work at a residential home for minors with functional diversity, where he unexpectedly finds acceptance. Producer David Aymerich calls it “a special coming-of-age story portraying a reality rarely seen on screen.” Selected at Locarno’s Match Me!, the project is set to shoot in March 2027.

	“Giant Stones,” (“Piedras gigantes,” Christopher Murray, Chile)

	The story of U.K. archaeologist Katherine Routledge’s arrival in 1914 on Rapa Nui to study its monumental moia statues and her conflictive role in an indigenous uprising. Winner of Hubert Bals Fund Development Support and set up at Fernando Bascuñan’s Planta which had three films at Cannes from Dominga Sotomayor (“La Perra”), Lisandro Alonso (“Double Freedom”) and Federico Luis (“For the Opponents”).



	

									‘The Illusions’
	



	“The Illusions,” (“Las ilusiones,” Ingrid Pokropek, Argentina-Spain)

	Three Buenos Aires strangers make wishes on a shooting star, only for a cosmic mix-up to grant each someone else’s desire, setting fame, grief and love on a collision course. Pokropek says “the world of ‘The Illusions’ is luminous in the middle of darkness.” 36 Caballos produces with Spain’s Jaibo Films. In advanced development for a fall 2027 shoot, the project has secured ICAA minority co-production support and passed through Berlinale Talents Project Market, EAVE Puentes and ECAM Forum.



	

									‘Isabel Hernández’
	



	“Isabel Hernández,” (Giorgio Giampà, Italy-Mexico)

	Seven years of research in Guatemala underpin Giampà’s first feature. “Working largely with non-professional actors whose own lives resonate with the story,” he says, the film follows a young agronomist searching for the truth about the father who abandoned her. Zoe Films and LaDoc produce with Mexico’s Fiasco. Set to shoot in autumn 2027, the project has passed through TorinoFilmLab FeatureLab and EAVE Producers Workshop.

	“The Last Cruise,” (“El último crucero,” Rachel Daisy Ellis, Brazil-Spain-Argentina)

	British-Brazilian filmmaker and longtime Gabriel Mascaro producer and creative collaborator Ellis turns to her own documentary work with “The Last Cruise,” a feature in development at Recife-based Desvia Filmes. Her directing debut, “Eros,” premiered at CPH:DOX, while she most recently produced Mascaro’s “The Blue Trail,” winner of Berlin’s Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize. Camile Reis produces alongside Ellis on the project.
	

	“Looking for Sam,” (“Buscando a Sam,” Mariana Rondón, Peru, Venezuela, Mexico)

	13 years after “Bad Hair,” Sam, its lead, has been forced to emigrate from Venezuela. Searching for him, director Rondón and producer Marité Ugas end up at the fashion catwalks Paris, discovering a tale of personal reinvention. “‘Looking For Sam’ wanders between fiction and documentary, where memory and identity blur and transform one another. It forces us to ask ourselves who we are when we leave behind who we once were,” says Rondón tells Variety.



	

									‘Modern Mermaids Revolution
	



	“Modern Mermaids Revolution,” (“La revolución de las sirenas modernas,” Azul Vanni, Uruguay-Argentina-Brazil)

	Vanni calls her feature debut “my own manifesto on how travesti and trans experiences can be represented in cinema.” Its protagonist, Sienna, loses her voice and begins growing scales after nearly drowning, entering an underground world of desire and danger. Uruguay’s Monarca Films produces alongside Argentina’s Groncho Estudio and Brazil’s Estudio Giz. Now financing for a first-half 2028 shoot, the project has passed through Tres Puertos, MECAS and Berlinale Talents Buenos Aires.

	“Mourning Sound,” (“El último sonidero,” Selma Cervantes, Mexico)

	After years abroad, Karina returns to Mexico following her mother’s death. Estranged from a country that no longer feels like home, she and her brother Nacho find a way to bridge their differences through their family’s tradition of being sonideros: DJs at popular neighbourhood dances. Cervantes’ first feature, following the success of her short film “Sweatshop Girl,” starring Yalitza Aparicio, which premiered at Sundance 2023.

	“Nature Boy,” (“O Estranho Meninho,” Matias Mariani, Brazil)

	A departure for Mariani? “Celestino, a São Paulo public-school principal whose life fits on a form, takes in a boy who speaks no known language — a boy who absorbs organic matter, transforms with everything he consumes, and is quietly studying the man learning, against his will, to be his father. the logline runs. A sci-fi family drama penned with “Shine Your Eyes” co-scribe Maíra Bühler from Primo Filmes and Tatiana Leite’s Bubbles Project. A title to track.

	“The Rehearsals,” (“Los Ensayos,” Celina Murga, Uruguay, Argentina) 
	

	Eva (48) accompanies her mother Emilia (80), a prestigious retired doctor facing the progression of Alzheimer’s. The family home is also shared by two caregivers, Eva’s teenage son and her younger sister. Amid improvised celebrations, hospital visits and conflicts over care, a mysterious presence of bulls surrounds the house. “Blending realism and the fantastic, the film explores fragility and the possibility of finding love and vitality in being there for another person,” while “reflecting on the way our society looks at aging, deterioration and death,” Murga told Variety.

	“They’re Taking Your Congos Away,” (“Te vienen a quitar tus congos,” Nelson Carlo De Los Santos Arias, Dominican Republic-Spain)

	One of the doyens of Dominican cinema, De Los Santos Arias returns after winning Berlin’s 2024 Silver Bear for Best Director with “Pepe.” His new project is an odyssey tracing the legacy of Spanish colonialism across the Caribbean. It is set up at Monte y Culebra, one of the Dominican Republic’s leading independent production companies.

	“This Is the Memory I Would Like to Have of Mom,” (“Este es el recuerdo que me gustaría tener de mamá,” Ernesto Martínez Bucio, Mexico, Spain)

	Next up from Martínez Bucio and screenwriter Karen Plata after scoring the Berlinale Perspectives first feature award with childhood survival tale “The Devil Smokes,” “a distinctive debut feature which steers what could be a familiar home-alone tale into darker psychological recesses,” Variety said in its review.

title: Michael Shannon Is Married Again, Weds Photographer Christy Bush

            Michael Shannon is a married man again ... tying the knot with photographer Christy Bush in Georgia.
      
    
            The actor and Bush got hitched in Athens earlier this month after obtaining a marriage license July 27, according to Page Six. The outlet reports the ceremony took place in Christy's hometown, with famous friends and other entertainment industry figures reportedly in attendance.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            It's unclear when Michael and Christy began dating or got engaged, though they have been spotted together several times over the past year. The couple visited Georgia's Pasaquan art compound in October 2025.
      

            The marriage comes after Michael quietly divorced his first wife, actress Kate Arrington, in 2022.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Michael and Kate began dating in 2002 after meeting through Chicago's theater scene. They welcomed daughters Sylvia in 2008 and Marion in 2014 before marrying in 2017.
      
    
            Christy was previously married to Interpol drummer Sam Fogarino, who she shares a daughter with.
      
    
            Congrats to the happy couple!!!

            Jenna Jameson is taking another stab at marriage ... because the ex-porn star has tied the knot with her partner Milagros Ocampo, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Jenna got hitched to Ocampo -- a voice actor and author -- in Miami, Florida, on July 25, 2026, after they secured a marriage license several weeks earlier, according to online records.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The lovebirds began dating in March 2025 just weeks after Jenna -- who is now a businesswoman -- filed for divorce from her former partner, Jessi Lawless. Jenna and Jessi were married in May 2023, but they separated less than a year later in April 2024.
      

            In an annulment filing, Jessi claimed that Jenna entered into the marriage under false pretenses, promising to be debt-free, among other things.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            But Jessi says Jenna never disclosed she was mired in a $500,000 tax debt before they said their "I Do's." Jessi also said Jenna pledged to stay sober, but she didn't keep her word. 
      
    
            Let's hope things go better for Jenna on the second go-around. Congrats, Jenna and Milagros!!!

title: Karoline Leavitt Is Stepping Down As White House Press Secretary
description:
Trump on Karoline Leavitt
                          Happy Trails To My Press Secretary
body:
Trump on Karoline Leavitt
                          Happy Trails To My Press Secretary
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                August 12, 2026
                
                            1:01 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 12, 2026
                                3:30 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Get ready for a new White House Press Secretary ... President Trump says Karoline Leavitt is stepping down from the job.
      
    
            Trump announced Karoline's upcoming career move in a Truth Social post Wednesday ... saying she's leaving the gig at the end of the month so she can spend more time with her kids and family.
      
    
            Karoline gave birth in May to a daughter ... her second child.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Trump says Karoline will be one of his top outside advisors and continue to be an influential voice within the GOP.
      

            It sounds like this is Karoline's choice ... Trump says he totally understands and respects her decision and praises her as one of the best White House Press Secretaries in American history.
      
    
            Karoline started her current role in January 2025, at the beginning of Trump's second term.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            No word who is on the short list to replace Karoline.
      
    
            Trump had 4 press secretaries in his first term ... and now he will have at least two in his second term.
      
    
            It will be interesting to see who lands the job.
      
    
            Stay tuned ...
